title: Āryabhaṭa's π
meter: Meter: Āryā (counted in mātrās: 30 + 27 per half-verse)
iast: caturadhikaṃ śatam aṣṭa-guṇaṃ dvāṣaṣṭis tathā sahasrāṇām |
translation: Add 4 to 100, multiply by 8, and add 62,000. This is the approximate circumference of a circle whose diameter is 20,000.
translation_hi: सौ में चार जोड़ो, आठ से गुणा करो और फिर बासठ हज़ार जोड़ो। यह बीस हज़ार व्यास वाले वृत्त की परिधि का निकटतम मान है।
grammar: Āsanna 'approximate': Āryabhaṭa calls his value 'near', not exact. Some historians read this as a sign he knew no exact fraction for π exists; π's irrationality was proved only in 1761.
Numbers as words: चतुरधिकं शतम् 'a hundred with four more' = 104. The verse is a recipe: (104 × 8) + 62000.
Genitive: विष्कम्भस्य 'of the diameter': the circumference belongs to that circle.
question: What value of π does this give, to four decimal places?
solution:
Circumference = (100 + 4) × 8 + 62000 = 832 + 62000 = 62832

π = circumference / diameter = 62832 / 20000 = 3.1416

True value: 3.14159265… Āryabhaṭa's value is correct to four decimal places.

Science link: choosing a diameter of 20,000 is clever: it turns π into a whole-number ratio with four exact decimals. The same trick, scaling up to avoid fractions, is what engineers do with per-unit values in power systems.
